html:
The Payómkawichum, better known as the Luiseño, are a Native people of coastal and inland northern San Diego County and southwestern Riverside County, California. The Spanish name comes from Mission San Luis Rey, founded in their land in 1798.

They speak a Uto-Aztecan language of the Takic branch. They lived in villages along streams, gathering acorns and seeds, hunting and fishing. Their religion included initiation rites for boys using a drink made from datura, and sand paintings of the world.

After Mexican and then American rule took most of their land, they were left on several small reservations, among them Pala, Pauma, Pechanga, Rincon and La Jolla. Their neighbours were the Acjachemen, Cupeño, Cahuilla and Kumeyaay. See also Luiseño and the Spanish missions in California.
